newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota to market green 'hybrid' cars worldwide.
newsitem.headline: Toyota to market green 'hybrid' cars worldwide.

text.p: Amid global concerns about greenhouse-gas emissions, Toyota Motor Corp is taking serious steps to market environmentally friendly "hybrid" cars, even though it expects the venture to register losses initially.

Toyota says it plans to introduce the vehicles, which combine a gasoline engine and an electric motor, in Japan later this year. It says it will be the first manufacturer in the world to introduce such a vehicle into the passenger market.

"Intially, far from making profits, I think the hybrid car will make losses. But if we mass-produce, it will not be a loss-making product for a long time," Akihiro Wada, an executive vice president in charge of research and development, told Reuters in a recent interview.

Toyota, Japan's biggest car marker, says the the new hybrid system vehicles will hit the road by the end of this year. It says their fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emission levels will be half those of comparable gasoline-powered vehicles, like its popular Corolla model.
It says other emissions, like those of nitrogen oxide and carbon monoxide, would be cut by a tenth.

"Right now, the hybrid car is much more practical than a purely electric vehicle (EV). EVs are not always zero emission vehicles in any case because electricity comes from power plants using fossil fuel and they have several big problems, like poor mileage and long recharging times," Wada said.

The hybrid car is started by its electric motor and the gasoline engine kicks in when the vehicle accelerates and is running at cruising speeds. The gasoline engine shuts off when the vehicle decelerates or comes to a halt. The gasoline engine recharges the batteries of the electric motor when in operation.

Wada said Toyota plans to market the hybrid in the United States and Europe as soon as possible after its launch in Japan, but added that it needed a year to 18 months to prove the reliability of the system in Japan, a country with a climate that is generally very tough for vehicles because of steep changes in temperature and high humidity.

On July 9, Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda pledged at a company forum on environmental issues that the firm would commit itself even more strongly to environmental issues from this year and should aim to take an industry lead.
President Bill Clinton launched a campaign on Thursday to win U.S. support for a global treaty to trim pollution from the burning of oil, coal and gas to help slow down global climate changes.

In March, European Union environment ministers agreed to cut the bloc's emissions of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide by 15 percent of 1990 levels by 2010, although Japan has said this target is too strict.
Wada said Toyota aimed to launch its hybrid cars at a price below three million yen ($25,600), or less than 500,000 yen ($4,273) more than an equivalent conventionally powered car.
Wada had no specific estimate on what sort of market share Toyota's hybrid cars would secure in future, but said:
"I am sure demand for hybrids will increase solidly; consumers will choose them because of fuel economy."
Asked if Toyota would aim to sell more than 1,000 units a month, he replied:
"We cannot be specific at the moment, but close to such a volume. We don't want to sell only 100 or 200 units (a month)."
He said Toyota planned to introduce a variety of hybrid models in the future.
Nissan Motor Co Ltd, Japan's second-biggest car maker, announced in May that it had developed a hybrid car. It said it hoped to market the vehicle by the end of 1998. (1$=117 yen)
